Let $p,d\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $f:\Theta\times W\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ and $g:W\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. Here $C^1$ means continuously differentiable on the open domain, and $C^2$ means that the derivative map is itself continuously differentiable. Gradients are column vectors, vector norms are Euclidean, and the norm of a matrix or linear map is the induced Euclidean operator norm.

For $(\theta,w)\in\Theta\times W$, define the inner stationarity residual $F(\theta,w):=\nabla_w f(\theta,w)\in\mathbb R^d$, its state Jacobian $H(\theta,w):=D_wF(\theta,w)\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$, and its parameter Jacobian $B(\theta,w):=D_\theta F(\theta,w)\in\mathbb R^{d\times p}$. Thus $H$ is the inner Hessian and $B$ is the mixed derivative of the inner gradient. A point $(\theta_0,w_0)$ is stationary when $F(\theta_0,w_0)=0$. If a $C^1$ map $w^*:P\to Q$, for open neighborhoods $P\subseteq\Theta$ of $\theta_0$ and $Q\subseteq W$ of $w_0$, satisfies $w^*(\theta_0)=w_0$ and $F(\theta,w^*(\theta))=0$ for all $\theta\in P$, it is a local stationary branch. The associated outer objective is $J(\theta):=g(w^*(\theta),\theta)$, and its column gradient $\nabla_\theta J$ is called the hypergradient of that branch. The definition of a local stationary branch imposes no global-minimality requirement.

For $\mu>0$, the phrase globally $\mu$-strongly convex in $w$ means that $f(\theta,\cdot)$ is defined on all of $\mathbb R^d$ and, for every $u,v\in\mathbb R^d$, satisfies

$$f(\theta,v)\ge f(\theta,u)+\nabla_w f(\theta,u)^T(v-u)+\frac{\mu}{2}\|v-u\|_2^2.$$

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n}$ be open, and let
$F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$.  Suppose $(a,b)\in U$, $F(a,b)=0$, and the
**partial derivative in the second block**

$$D_yF(a,b):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n,\qquad D_yF(a,b)v:=DF(a,b)(0,v),$$

is invertible.  Put similarly $D_xF(a,b)u:=DF(a,b)(u,0)$.  Then there are open
neighbourhoods $P$ of $a$ and $Q$ of $b$, and a unique $C^1$ map
$\varphi:P\to Q$, such that

$$F(x,y)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x)\qquad((x,y)\in P\times Q).$$

After shrinking $P,Q$ if necessary, $D_yF(x,\varphi(x))$ is invertible and

$$D\varphi(x)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x))^{-1}D_xF(x,\varphi(x)).$$

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n}$ be open, and let
$F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$.  Suppose $(a,b)\in U$, $F(a,b)=0$, and the
**partial derivative in the second block**

$$D_yF(a,b):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n,\qquad D_yF(a,b)v:=DF(a,b)(0,v),$$

is invertible.  Put similarly $D_xF(a,b)u:=DF(a,b)(u,0)$.  Then there are open
neighbourhoods $P$ of $a$ and $Q$ of $b$, and a unique $C^1$ map
$\varphi:P\to Q$, such that

$$F(x,y)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x)\qquad((x,y)\in P\times Q).$$

After shrinking $P,Q$ if necessary, $D_yF(x,\varphi(x))$ is invertible and

$$D\varphi(x)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x))^{-1}D_xF(x,\varphi(x)).$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: Put $F(\theta,w)=\nabla_w f(\theta,w)$. Since $f$ is $C^2$, this residual is $C^1$ on the open product domain; it vanishes at $(\theta_0,w_0)$ and its state derivative is the invertible matrix $H(\theta_0,w_0)$. Applying [F2] gives open neighborhoods and a unique $C^1$ local branch $w^*$ through that point.
The derivative clause of [L1], evaluated along this branch after shrinking its parameter neighborhood, gives $Dw^*(\theta)=-H(\theta,w^*(\theta))^{-1}B(\theta,w^*(\theta))$.
The map $\theta\mapsto (w^*(\theta),\theta)$ is $C^1$, so [F3] applied to $g$ and this map yields $\nabla_\theta J=\partial_\theta g+(Dw^*)^T\nabla_w g$.
Substitute step 2.1 into step 2.2 and use $(H^{-1}B)^T=B^TH^{-T}$. This is the asserted column-gradient hypergradient formula.

In the stated global regime, fix any $\theta\in P$ and any stationary point $u\in\mathbb R^d$, so $\nabla_w f(\theta,u)=0$. For every $v\ne u$, the strong-convexity inequality gives $f(\theta,v)\ge f(\theta,u)+\frac{\mu}{2}\|v-u\|_2^2>f(\theta,u)$. Thus this arbitrary stationary point is the unique global minimizer, proving the claim for every stationary point wherever the global regime holds.

Let $p,d\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $f:\Theta\times W\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ and $g:W\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. Here $C^1$ means continuously differentiable on the open domain, and $C^2$ means that the derivative map is itself continuously differentiable. Gradients are column vectors, vector norms are Euclidean, and the norm of a matrix or linear map is the induced Euclidean operator norm.

Thus $H$ is the inner Hessian and $B$ is the mixed derivative of the inner gradient. A point $(\theta_0,w_0)$ is stationary when $F(\theta_0,w_0)=0$. If a $C^1$ map $w^*:P\to Q$, for open neighborhoods $P\subseteq\Theta$ of $\theta_0$ and $Q\subseteq W$ of $w_0$, satisfies $w^*(\theta_0)=w_0$ and $F(\theta,w^*(\theta))=0$ for all $\theta\in P$, it is a local stationary branch. The associated outer objective is $J(\theta):=g(w^*(\theta),\theta)$, and its column gradient $\nabla_\theta J$ is called the hypergradient of that branch. The definition of a local stationary branch imposes no global-minimality requirement.

For $\mu>0$, the phrase globally $\mu$-strongly convex in $w$ means that $f(\theta,\cdot)$ is defined on all of $\mathbb R^d$ and, for every $u,v\in\mathbb R^d$, satisfies

$$f(\theta,v)\ge f(\theta,u)+\nabla_w f(\theta,u)^T(v-u)+\frac{\mu}{2}\|v-u\|_2^2.$$

Let $p,d\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $f:\Theta\times W\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ and $g:W\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. Here $C^1$ means total differentiability with continuous derivative, and $C^2$ means the derivative map is $C^1$. Define $F(\theta,w)=\nabla_w f(\theta,w)$, $H(\theta,w)=D_wF(\theta,w)$, and $B(\theta,w)=D_\theta F(\theta,w)$. Suppose $F(\theta_0,w_0)=0$ and $H(\theta_0,w_0)$ is invertible. Then there are open neighborhoods $P\subseteq\Theta$ and $Q\subseteq W$ of $\theta_0$ and $w_0$ and a unique $C^1$ local stationary branch $w^*:P\to Q$ through $(\theta_0,w_0)$, meaning $w^*(\theta_0)=w_0$ and $F(\theta,w^*(\theta))=0$ for every $\theta\in P$. After shrinking $P$ if necessary, $H(\theta,w^*(\theta))$ is invertible and

$$Dw^*(\theta)=-H(\theta,w^*(\theta))^{-1}B(\theta,w^*(\theta)).$$

Write $H^{-T}:=(H^{-1})^T$. For $J(\theta)=g(w^*(\theta),\theta)$, where $\partial_\theta g$ holds $w$ fixed and gradients are column vectors, the hypergradient is

$$\nabla_\theta J(\theta)=\partial_\theta g(w^*(\theta),\theta)-B(\theta,w^*(\theta))^T H(\theta,w^*(\theta))^{-T}\nabla_w g(w^*(\theta),\theta).$$

The local branch need not be a global inner optimizer. In the separate global regime where, for every $\theta\in P$, $f(\theta,\cdot)$ is defined on all of $\mathbb R^d$ and, for some $\mu>0$, satisfies $f(\theta,v)\ge f(\theta,u)+\nabla_w f(\theta,u)^T(v-u)+\frac{\mu}{2}\|v-u\|_2^2$ for every $u,v\in\mathbb R^d$, each stationary point is the unique global minimizer.

Let $R(z,\theta)$ be $C^2$ near an exact solution $R(z_*,\theta_0)=0$, with $A(z)=R_z(z,\theta_0)$ invertible and $B(z)=R_\theta(z,\theta_0)$. The implicit sensitivity at a state $z$ is $S(z)=-A(z)^{-1}B(z)$. Suppose the local inverse $\Psi$ of $z\mapsto R(z,\theta_0)$, supplied near $z_*$ by the implicit function theorem, is defined on a convex residual neighborhood containing $0$ and $r=R(\tilde z,\theta_0)$, with $\|D\Psi(y)\|\le\kappa$ along their segment. Suppose also that the segment from $z_*$ to $\tilde z=\Psi(r)$ lies in a convex neighborhood where $\|A(z)^{-1}\|\le M$, $\|B(z)\|\le B_0$, and $A,B$ are Lipschitz with constants $L_A,L_B$. Then
$$\|S(\tilde z)-S(z_*)\|\le\kappa\bigl(M^2L_AB_0+ML_B\bigr)\|r\|.$$
This bounds the implicit sensitivity formula evaluated at an approximate state. It is not by itself a bound for the derivative of a stopped iteration.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Input positive dimensions $p,d$, open sets $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $C^2$ and $C^1$ scalar functions $f:\Theta\times W\to\mathbb R$ and $g:W\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$, a point $(\theta,w)\in\Theta\times W$, and finite real-arithmetic computational graphs whose outputs equal $f$ and $g$ on open neighborhoods of the evaluated inputs. The graph primitives for $f$ are $C^2$ and those for $g$ are $C^1$. Here $C^1$ means total differentiability with continuous derivative, $C^2$ means the derivative map is $C^1$, and all graph evaluations must remain on one unique strict branch. Define $F=\nabla_w f$, $H=D_wF$, $B=D_\theta F$, $c=\partial_\theta g$ with $w$ held fixed, and $d=\nabla_w g$; all gradients are column vectors. Also input a tolerance $\tau\ge0$, a positive integer solve budget $N$, a number $\mu>0$, and a valid certificate that the evaluated inner Hessian is symmetric and satisfies $x^THx\ge\mu\|x\|_2^2$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$. Finally input a deterministic solver $S$ with the following contract: on a real symmetric positive-definite linear operator and a right-hand side, $S$ terminates within $N$ iterations and returns either a failure status or a vector $\widetilde v$ and a report saying whether its own stopping test passed. The algorithm does not trust that report as an accuracy certificate; it recomputes the residual. All derivative and solver operations in this definition use exact real arithmetic.

If any graph evaluation is outside its declared domain, return DOMAIN_ERROR. If any piecewise primitive is at a branch boundary or has no unique strict active branch, return NONDIFFERENTIABLE and no gradient. Otherwise, use reverse mode on $f$ and take the state block of its returned gradient as the inner residual $r_{\rm in}:=\nabla_w f(\theta,w)$. Use reverse mode on $g$ and take its parameter and state blocks as $c:=\partial_\theta g(w,\theta)$ and $d:=\nabla_w g(w,\theta)$. In these expressions $c$ is the derivative with $w$ held fixed, and $d$ and $c$ are column vectors.

For any $u\in\mathbb R^d$, apply forward-over-reverse Hessian-vector differentiation to $f$ at $(\theta,w)$ in direction $(0,u)\in\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^d$. Let $\pi_\theta$ and $\pi_w$ denote projection onto the parameter and state coordinates of the returned vector. Define $M_Hu:=\pi_w\bigl(D(\nabla f)(\theta,w)(0,u)\bigr)$ and $M_Bu:=\pi_\theta\bigl(D(\nabla f)(\theta,w)(0,u)\bigr)$. Hessian symmetry makes $M_Hu=Hu=H^Tu$ and $M_Bu=B^Tu$.

Call $S$ on $M_H$ and right-hand side $d$ with tolerance $\tau$ and budget $N$. If $S$ returns failure, return $(r_{\rm in},\text{SOLVER\_FAILURE})$ with no hypergradient. If it returns a vector $\widetilde v$, compute the actual linear residual $\rho:=d-M_H\widetilde v$ and the reported hypergradient estimate $\widehat h:=c-M_B\widetilde v$. Return $(\widehat h,r_{\rm in},\rho,\text{CONVERGED})$ exactly when the solver reports its stopping test passed and $\|\rho\|_2\le\tau$; otherwise return the same numerical values with status TOLERANCE_OR_BUDGET_NOT_MET. The procedure makes no floating-point accuracy claim.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: Put $S(w):=-A(w)^{-1}B(w)$ on the stated state neighborhood. The chart and Lipschitz hypotheses with [F3] give $\|S(\widetilde w)-S(w^*)\|\le\kappa(M^2L_AB_0+ML_B)\|r\|_2$.

For the state bound, set $\gamma(t):=\Psi(tr)$ for $0<t<1$. By [F4], $\gamma'(t)=D\Psi(tr)r$, so $\|\gamma'(t)\|_2\le\kappa\|r\|_2$. For $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, apply [F5] to $\gamma$ on the convex open interval $(\varepsilon/2,1-\varepsilon/2)$ at $\varepsilon$ and $1-\varepsilon$; it gives $\|\Psi((1-\varepsilon)r)-\Psi(\varepsilon r)\|_2\le\kappa(1-2\varepsilon)\|r\|_2$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and using continuity of $\Psi$, $\Psi(0)=w^*$ and $\Psi(r)=\widetilde w$ give $\|\widetilde w-w^*\|_2\le\kappa\|r\|_2$.
The inverse and operator-norm hypotheses give $\|S(\widetilde w)\|\le\|A(\widetilde w)^{-1}\|\,\|B(\widetilde w)\|\le MB_0$.

Define the implicit formula evaluated at a state by $\bar h(w):=c(w)+S(w)^Td(w)$. By [F1] and [F2], $\bar h(w^*)=\nabla_\theta J(\theta_0)$. Expansion gives $\bar h(\widetilde w)-\bar h(w^*)=(c(\widetilde w)-c(w^*))+(S(\widetilde w)-S(w^*))^Td(w^*)+S(\widetilde w)^T(d(\widetilde w)-d(w^*))$.

At the evaluated state, write $H=A(\widetilde w)$ and $B=B(\theta_0,\widetilde w)$. Let $v_*=H^{-T}d(\widetilde w)$. The residual identity gives $v_*-\widetilde v=H^{-T}\rho$. For any vector $x$, the certificate and [F7] imply $\mu\|x\|_2^2\le x^THx\le\|x\|_2\|Hx\|_2$, hence $\|H^{-1}\|\le1/\mu$; symmetry gives the same bound for $H^{-T}$. The Euclidean dual formula and [F7] give $\|B^Ty\|_2\le\|B\|\|y\|_2$, so $\|\widehat h-\bar h(\widetilde w)\|_2=\|B^TH^{-T}\rho\|_2\le(B_0/\mu)\|\rho\|_2$.

For the exact-state claim, put $H:=H(\theta_0,w_0)$, $B:=B(\theta_0,w_0)$, $c:=c(w_0)$, and $d:=d(w_0)$, and let $v_*:=H^{-T}d$. Since $w_0=w^*(\theta_0)$, [F2] gives $\nabla_\theta J(\theta_0)=c-B^Tv_*$. The residual identity gives $v_*-\widetilde v=H^{-T}\rho$. For every $x$, the stated symmetry and lower-bound certificate together with [F7] imply $\mu\|x\|_2^2\le x^THx\le\|x\|_2\|Hx\|_2$, so $\|H^{-1}\|\le1/\mu$; symmetry gives $\|H^{-T}\|\le1/\mu$. The Euclidean dual formula and [F7] give $\|B^Ty\|_2\le\|B\|\|y\|_2$. Therefore $$\|\widehat h-\nabla_\theta J(\theta_0)\|_2=\|B^TH^{-T}\rho\|_2\le\frac{\|B\|\,\|\rho\|_2}{\mu}=\frac{\|B(\theta_0,w^*(\theta_0))\|\,\|\rho\|_2}{\mu}.$$ This proves the exact-state claim using only its stated hypotheses.

For any matrix $M$ and vector $x$, the Euclidean dual formula $\|M^Tx\|_2=\sup_{\|y\|_2=1}|y^TM^Tx|$ and [F7] give $\|M^Tx\|_2\le\|M\|\|x\|_2$. Apply this to the two transpose terms in step 1.4, then use the triangle inequality, the stated Lipschitz bounds for $c,d$, the bound $\|d(w^*)\|_2\le D_*$, and steps 1.1–1.3 to obtain $\|\bar h(\widetilde w)-\nabla_\theta J(\theta_0)\|_2\le\bigl(L_c+D_*(M^2L_AB_0+ML_B)+MB_0L_d\bigr)\|\widetilde w-w^*\|_2$.
Substitute the state-residual estimate from step 1.2 into step 2.1. This gives the first term in the asserted approximate-state bound for the implicit formula evaluation.

Combine the approximate-state formula bound from step 3.1 and the solve-error bound from step 1.5 by the triangle inequality. This gives the approximate-state bound under its separate chart and Lipschitz hypotheses.

derivations.claim: Differentiate the inner loss: $\partial_wf=(1+\lambda)w-1$ and $H=1+\lambda>0$. Thus its stationary point is $w^*=1/(1+\lambda)$. Completing the square gives $f(\lambda,w)=\frac12(1+\lambda)(w-\frac1{1+\lambda})^2+\frac{\lambda}{2(1+\lambda)}$, so this stationary point is the unique global minimizer.
Substitution into the outer loss gives $J(\lambda)=1/(2(1+\lambda)^2)$, whose direct derivative is $J'(\lambda)=-1/(1+\lambda)^3$.

At $w^*$, the mixed derivative is $B=\partial_\lambda((1+\lambda)w-1)=w^*=1/(1+\lambda)$, the state derivative is $\nabla_wg=w^*=1/(1+\lambda)$, and $\partial_\lambda g=0$. Formula [F2] therefore gives $-B H^{-1}\nabla_wg=-1/(1+\lambda)^3$, agreeing with step 2.1.

Let $p,d\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $f:\Theta\times W\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ and $g:W\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. Here $C^1$ means continuously differentiable on the open domain, and $C^2$ means that the derivative map is itself continuously differentiable. Gradients are column vectors, vector norms are Euclidean, and the norm of a matrix or linear map is the induced Euclidean operator norm.

For $(\theta,w)\in\Theta\times W$, define the inner stationarity residual $F(\theta,w):=\nabla_w f(\theta,w)\in\mathbb R^d$, its state Jacobian $H(\theta,w):=D_wF(\theta,w)\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$, and its parameter Jacobian $B(\theta,w):=D_\theta F(\theta,w)\in\mathbb R^{d\times p}$. Thus $H$ is the inner Hessian and $B$ is the mixed derivative of the inner gradient. A point $(\theta_0,w_0)$ is stationary when $F(\theta_0,w_0)=0$. If a $C^1$ map $w^*:P\to Q$, for open neighborhoods $P\subseteq\Theta$ of $\theta_0$ and $Q\subseteq W$ of $w_0$, satisfies $w^*(\theta_0)=w_0$ and $F(\theta,w^*(\theta))=0$ for all $\theta\in P$, it is a local stationary branch. The associated outer objective is $J(\theta):=g(w^*(\theta),\theta)$, and its column gradient $\nabla_\theta J$ is called the hypergradient of that branch. The definition of a local stationary branch imposes no global-minimality requirement.

For $\mu>0$, the phrase globally $\mu$-strongly convex in $w$ means that $f(\theta,\cdot)$ is defined on all of $\mathbb R^d$ and, for every $u,v\in\mathbb R^d$, satisfies

$$f(\theta,v)\ge f(\theta,u)+\nabla_w f(\theta,u)^T(v-u)+\frac{\mu}{2}\|v-u\|_2^2.$$

Let $p,d\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $f:\Theta\times W\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ and $g:W\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. Here $C^1$ means total differentiability with continuous derivative, and $C^2$ means the derivative map is $C^1$. Define $F(\theta,w)=\nabla_w f(\theta,w)$, $H(\theta,w)=D_wF(\theta,w)$, and $B(\theta,w)=D_\theta F(\theta,w)$. Suppose $F(\theta_0,w_0)=0$ and $H(\theta_0,w_0)$ is invertible. Then there are open neighborhoods $P\subseteq\Theta$ and $Q\subseteq W$ of $\theta_0$ and $w_0$ and a unique $C^1$ local stationary branch $w^*:P\to Q$ through $(\theta_0,w_0)$, meaning $w^*(\theta_0)=w_0$ and $F(\theta,w^*(\theta))=0$ for every $\theta\in P$. After shrinking $P$ if necessary, $H(\theta,w^*(\theta))$ is invertible and

$$Dw^*(\theta)=-H(\theta,w^*(\theta))^{-1}B(\theta,w^*(\theta)).$$

Write $H^{-T}:=(H^{-1})^T$. For $J(\theta)=g(w^*(\theta),\theta)$, where $\partial_\theta g$ holds $w$ fixed and gradients are column vectors, the hypergradient is

$$\nabla_\theta J(\theta)=\partial_\theta g(w^*(\theta),\theta)-B(\theta,w^*(\theta))^T H(\theta,w^*(\theta))^{-T}\nabla_w g(w^*(\theta),\theta).$$

The local branch need not be a global inner optimizer. In the separate global regime where, for every $\theta\in P$, $f(\theta,\cdot)$ is defined on all of $\mathbb R^d$ and, for some $\mu>0$, satisfies $f(\theta,v)\ge f(\theta,u)+\nabla_w f(\theta,u)^T(v-u)+\frac{\mu}{2}\|v-u\|_2^2$ for every $u,v\in\mathbb R^d$, each stationary point is the unique global minimizer.

derivations.claim: The inner loss is nonnegative and equals zero exactly when $u=\theta$, independently of $v$. Therefore its full global minimizer set is $\{(\theta,v):v\in\mathbb R\}$.
Its state gradient is $(u-\theta,0)^T$ and its Hessian is $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, whose kernel contains $(0,1)^T$ and is therefore singular.

The maps $w_0^*(\theta)=(\theta,0)$ and $w_1^*(\theta)=(\theta,\theta)$ are both $C^1$ and lie in the minimizing set from step 1.1 for every $\theta$. Their outer objectives are $g(w_0^*(\theta),\theta)=0$ and $g(w_1^*(\theta),\theta)=\theta$, so their derivatives are respectively $0$ and $1$.

Since these two admissible selections yield distinct derivatives and step 1.2 violates the invertibility hypothesis in [F2], the input does not determine one hypergradient through the argmin set, and the local formula does not apply.

Let $p,m\ge0$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ be open with $\theta_0\in\Theta$, and let $G:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^2$ on an open neighborhood $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m\times\Theta$ of $D\times\{\theta_0\}$. Suppose $D\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is an open convex neighborhood of $z_*$ and $z_*=G(z_*,\theta_0)$. Assume $G(D,\theta_0)\subseteq D$, $\|G_z(z,\theta_0)\|\le q<1$ on $D$, and $G_z,G_\theta$ are Lipschitz in $z$ with constants $L_z,L_\theta$. Let $z_0:\Theta\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$, with the iterates at $\theta_0$ lying in $D$. Write $s_*=D\phi(\theta_0)$ for the local exact fixed-point branch (supplied by the implicit function theorem when $p,m\ge1$), $e_k=D_\theta z_k(\theta_0)$, $\delta_0=\|z_0(\theta_0)-z_*\|$, $d_0=\|e_0-s_*\|$, and $C=L_z\|s_*\|+L_\theta$. For every integer $K\ge1$,
$$\|z_K(\theta_0)-z_*\|\le q^K\delta_0,\qquad \|e_K-s_*\|\le q^K d_0+C K q^{K-1}\delta_0,$$
with $q^0=1$ when $q=0,K=1$. If $R(z,\theta)=z-G(z,\theta)$ and $r_K=R(z_K(\theta_0),\theta_0)$, then $(1-q)\|z_K-z_*\|\le\|r_K\|$. The derivative error is not bounded by the residual alone: for $G(z,\theta)=qz+(1-q)\theta$, $\theta_0=0$, and $z_0(\theta)=0$, every finite $K$ has residual zero at $\theta_0$ but $e_K=1-q^K\ne1=s_*$ when $0<q<1$.

derivations.claim: Solving $z=G(z,\theta)$ gives $(1-q)z=(1-q)\theta$. Since $1-q>0$, the unique fixed point is $z^*(\theta)=\theta$, and therefore $J(\theta)=z^*(\theta)$ has derivative $1$. Also $G_z=q<1$.

For $K=0$, $z_0(\theta)=(1-q^0)\theta=0$. If $z_K(\theta)=(1-q^K)\theta$, then $z_{K+1}=q(1-q^K)\theta+(1-q)\theta=(1-q^{K+1})\theta$. Induction gives the displayed finite-iterate formula for every $K\ge1$.

The inner objective has $\partial_zf=z-\theta$, so its stationary branch is the same $z^*(\theta)=\theta$ as the fixed-point branch. Here $H=1$, $B=-1$, $\partial_\theta g=0$, and $\nabla_zg=1$. Formula [F3] therefore gives $0-(-1)(1)^{-1}(1)=1$, verifying the exact hypergradient under the bilevel prerequisites.

At $\theta_0=0$, step 1.2 gives $z_K(0)=0=z^*(0)$ and the fixed-point residual is $z_K(0)-G(z_K(0),0)=0-G(0,0)=0$. The stopped outer objective is $J_K(\theta)=g(z_K(\theta),\theta)=(1-q^K)\theta$, so $J_K'(0)=1-q^K$.
Because $0<q<1$ and $K\ge1$, $q^K>0$, hence $1-q^K\ne1$. Thus the zero residual at the exact state does not make the finite-unroll derivative equal to the exact hypergradient.
